title: Gravity energy storage economics
bottleneck: Gravity storage, lifting masses with surplus power, is mechanically simple and long-lived, but energy density is abysmal: storing meaningful energy requires thousands of tonnes lifted hundreds of meters. Capital costs per kWh remain high, round-trip efficiency is modest, and suitable sites or structures add expense. It competes against pumped hydro where geography allows and loses everywhere else. Round-trip efficiency through mechanical systems typically lands between 70 and 85 percent, acceptable but not compelling against batteries.
why_it_blocks: Gravity storage's physics caps its relevance. Without extreme scale it stores trivial energy, and at extreme scale it costs more than alternatives.
current_state: Pilot projects using cranes, mine shafts, and rail are operating or under construction. No project has demonstrated competitive levelized costs.
